ecb-2026-09.standing: The European Central Bank's Governing Council, which sets interest rates for the euro area roughly every six weeks. Its decisions set the cost of borrowing for twenty countries and transmit through the euro's exchange rate to everyone trading against it.
ecb-2026-09.recent: The Council meets into a global bond selloff that carried yields to multi-decade highs on inflation fears, with the dollar at its weakest since May and the yen surging — moves that reach the euro area through import prices rather than through domestic demand. Other central banks have already turned: the Bank of Korea hiked to 3.00%, and markets have swung toward a September hike in Washington.

fomc-2026-09.standing: The rate-setting committee of the US Federal Reserve, which meets eight times a year to set the target range for overnight lending between banks. Its decisions set the cost of dollar borrowing worldwide, and every asset priced in dollars moves with them.
fomc-2026-09.recent: An oil shock has turned the question from a cut to a hike, and the committee has to decide whether a supply-driven price rise deserves the same answer as a demand-driven one. A payroll surge pushed hike odds to two-in-three, and Warsh has staked his early tenure on the answer.

boe-2026-09.standing: The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee, which meets eight times a year to set Bank Rate, the anchor for borrowing costs across the British economy. Its votes are published individually, so the split itself is information.
boe-2026-09.recent: Governor Andrew Bailey has spent the run-up warning the G20 that AI models pose new risks to financial stability rather than arguing about prices — a committee talking about something other than inflation as a global bond selloff pushes yields to multi-decade highs. The vote will settle how much of that selloff the committee treats as its own problem.

boj-2026-09.standing: Japan's central bank, whose policy board meets eight times a year to set the short-term policy rate and guide long-term yields. Its decisions set the price of the world's largest pool of cheap funding, and move the yen against every major currency.
boj-2026-09.recent: The yen fell past 160 per dollar before this meeting, a level that has previously drawn intervention, and the gap between Japanese and foreign policy rates is what is driving it. The Bank of Korea has already hiked to 3.00% citing financial stability, and markets have moved to favor a September hike in Washington — leaving Tokyo to decide whether to close the gap or defend the currency another way.

uk-cpi-2026-10.standing: The Office for National Statistics' monthly measure of UK consumer price inflation, published a few weeks after the month it covers. It anchors the Bank of England's rate decisions and is used to uprate pensions, benefits and index-linked government debt.

Warsh has framed the choice as one about imported inflation and the dollar. A payroll surge has already pushed hike odds to two-in-three.

ecb-2026-10.standing: The European Central Bank's Governing Council, which meets roughly every six weeks to set interest rates for the euro area. Its decisions set the cost of borrowing across the single-currency bloc and move the euro.

boe-2026-11.standing: The United Kingdom's central bank, whose Monetary Policy Committee meets eight times a year to set Bank Rate. That rate sets the floor for British mortgage and business borrowing costs, and moves the pound against other currencies.
boe-2026-11.recent: Governor Andrew Bailey has spent the run-up warning the G20 that AI could cause a global economic downturn and that AI models pose new risks to financial stability — an unusual framing for a committee whose job is the domestic price level. g20-2026-miami.standing: The annual meeting of heads of state and government from the world's twenty largest economies, plus the European Union. It has no treaty powers, so its output is a consensus communiqué — which makes agreement itself the test, and a walkout a substantive result.
g20-2026-miami.recent: The US presidency has spent the run-up rallying the G20 against China's trade surplus while welcoming Russia back, and European finance ministers already boycotted the family photo in Asheville over Siluanov's return. Wang Yi has told Washington to "remove disruptions." What Asheville settles is whether a consensus body still produces consensus.

ecb-2026-12.standing: The euro area's central bank, whose Governing Council sets the deposit and refinancing rates for the twenty countries that share the currency. Its decisions set borrowing costs across the bloc and anchor how the euro trades against other currencies.
ecb-2026-12.recent: This is the last decision of the year, and it comes after a global bond selloff that pushed yields to multi-decade highs on inflation fears. The euro's side of that move matters: the dollar has fallen to its weakest since May, which cuts the imported-inflation pressure the Council has been weighing.

boe-2026-12.standing: The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee, which meets eight times a year to set Bank Rate. Its decisions set the cost of borrowing across the sterling economy, feeding through to mortgages, business credit and the pound.

boj-2026-12.standing: Japan's central bank, whose policy board sets the short-term policy rate and shapes the yield curve. Its decisions move the yen, the cost of credit in Japan, and the carry trades that link Japanese savings to markets abroad.
boj-2026-12.recent: The yen fell past 160 per dollar in August, a level that has drawn intervention before, and the gap between Japanese rates and those abroad is what drives it. The board has to weigh whether energy costs passing through a weak currency call for tightening, while the Bank of Korea has already hiked twice and Washington is now favoring a hike of its own.

fred-us-ppi-2026-09-10.standing: The US producer price index, published monthly by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, measuring the prices domestic producers receive for their output. It reads cost pressure upstream of consumer inflation and feeds parts of the Fed's preferred gauge.
fred-us-ppi-2026-09-10.recent: The Bureau of Labor Statistics reports what US producers were paid over the past month, settling how much cost pressure is sitting upstream of the consumer price data. Nothing on the record sets this release apart from a routine one.

fred-us-cpi-2026-09-11.standing: The Bureau of Labor Statistics' monthly consumer price index, the most-watched measure of what American households pay for goods and services. It sets the reference rate for inflation-linked contracts and is the number the Federal Reserve is judged against.
fred-us-cpi-2026-09-11.recent: This release lands with the Fed's own question inverted: an oil shock has moved the argument from a cut toward a hike, and payroll strength has pushed hike odds to roughly two-in-three. Warsh has framed the trap as imported inflation the Fed cannot source domestically, so the print settles whether price pressure is broad or confined to energy.
